title: Book 1, Chapter 1 — The State of Greece from the earliest Times to the Commencement of the Peloponnesian War
paragraphs: Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians. He began his work the moment the war broke out, believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of being recorded than any before it. He had good grounds for this belief. Both sides were at the very peak of preparation in every department, and he could see the rest of the Hellenic race taking sides in the quarrel, some at once and others planning to do so. Indeed this was the greatest upheaval yet known in history, affecting not only the Hellenes but a large part of the barbarian world — I had almost said mankind. The events of remote antiquity, and even those just before the war, could not be known clearly because of the time that has passed. Yet the evidence that I trust after carrying my inquiry as far back as was practicable all points to one conclusion: that nothing on a great scale happened in those times, either in war or in other matters.

For instance, it is clear that the country now called Hellas had no settled population in ancient times. Migrations were frequent, and each tribe readily left its home when a larger force pressed it. There was no commerce and no safe communication by land or sea. People cultivated only as much land as they needed to live on, and they had no capital. They never even planted their land, for they could not tell when an invader might come and take it all away, and when he did come they had no walls to stop him. Thinking that daily necessities could be supplied in one place as well as in another, they cared little about moving, and so they built no large cities and reached no other form of greatness. The richest soils were always the most liable to change of masters, such as the district now called Thessaly, Boeotia, most of Peloponnese except Arcadia, and the most fertile parts of the rest of Hellas. The goodness of the land favored the aggrandizement of particular individuals, and this created faction, a fertile source of ruin. It also invited invasion. Attica, by contrast, had a poor soil and from a very remote period was free from faction, and so it never changed its inhabitants. And here is no small proof of my claim that migrations kept the other parts from growing in the same way. The most powerful men driven out by war or faction from the rest of Hellas took refuge with the Athenians as a safe retreat. Early on they became citizens, and they swelled the city’s population, already large, until Attica could no longer hold them and they had to send out colonies to Ionia.

Another circumstance contributes a good deal to my conviction that ancient times were weak. Before the Trojan war there is no sign of any common action in Hellas, nor even of the name being used for the whole country. On the contrary, before the time of Hellen, son of Deucalion, no such name existed, and the country went by the names of its different tribes, above all the Pelasgian. Only when Hellen and his sons grew strong in Phthiotis and were invited into the other cities as allies did those cities, one by one, gradually take the name of Hellenes from the connection. A long time passed before the name could attach itself to all. Homer furnishes the best proof of this. He was born long after the Trojan War, yet he nowhere calls them all by that name, nor any of them except the followers of Achilles from Phthiotis, who were the original Hellenes. In his poems they are called Danaans, Argives, and Achaeans. He does not even use the word barbarian, probably because the Hellenes had not yet been set apart from the rest of the world by a single distinctive name. It appears, then, that the Hellenic communities were unable to act together before the Trojan war, for want of strength and of mutual contact. These communities include both those that first took the name city by city as they came to understand each other, and those that adopted it afterwards as the name of the whole people.

Indeed, they could not even unite for this expedition until they had become more familiar with the sea. The first person known to us by tradition as having established a navy is Minos. He became master of what is now called the Hellenic sea and ruled over the Cyclades. He sent the first colonies into most of them, expelling the Carians and appointing his own sons as governors. In this way he did his best to put down piracy in those waters, a step he needed to secure his own revenues.

For in early times, as communication by sea became more common, the Hellenes and the barbarians of the coast and islands were tempted to turn to piracy, led by their most powerful men. Their motives were their own greed and the support of the needy. They would fall on a town that had no walls and was a mere collection of villages, and plunder it. This became their main source of livelihood, since no disgrace was yet attached to such an exploit, and it even brought some glory. As an illustration, some people on the mainland still honor a successful raider. So do the old poets, who everywhere show people asking voyagers the question “Are they pirates?” — as if those asked would never think of denying the charge, and those who asked would never think of reproaching them for it. The same plundering went on by land as well.

Even today many parts of Hellas still follow the old fashion: the Ozolian Locrians, for instance, the Aetolians, the Acarnanians, and that region of the mainland. The custom of carrying arms survives among these mainlanders from their old piratical habits. All of Hellas once carried arms, because their dwellings were unprotected and travel between places was unsafe. Wearing arms was as much a part of everyday life for them as for the barbarians. And the fact that the people in these parts of Hellas still live in the old way points to a time when the same way of life was common to all. The Athenians were the first to lay down their weapons and adopt an easier, more luxurious way of life. It is only recently that their rich old men stopped wearing undergarments of linen and fastening a knot of their hair with a tie of golden grasshoppers. This fashion spread to their Ionian kindred and long prevailed among the old men there. The Lacedaemonians, on the other hand, were the first to adopt a modest style of dress, closer to modern ideas, and their rich did their best to bring their way of life level with that of the common people. They also set the example of competing naked, stripping and anointing themselves with oil in public at their gymnastic exercises. Formerly, even at the Olympic contests, the athletes wore belts across their middles, and the practice ceased only a few years ago. To this day among some of the barbarians, especially in Asia, the contestants wear belts when prizes for boxing and wrestling are offered. Many other points could be shown in which the life of the old Hellenic world resembled that of the barbarians today.

As for their towns, later on, when navigation was easier and capital more plentiful, we find walled towns built on the shores, and isthmuses occupied for the sake of commerce and defense against a neighbor. But the old towns, because piracy was so widespread, were built away from the sea, whether on the islands or on the mainland, and they still stand on their old sites. For the pirates used to plunder one another, and in fact all coast populations, whether seafaring or not.

The islanders, too, were great pirates. These islanders were Carians and Phoenicians, who had colonized most of the islands, as the following fact proves. When Athens purified Delos in this war, all the graves in the island were opened, and more than half of their occupants were found to be Carians. They were identified by the style of the arms buried with them and by the manner of burial, which is the same as the Carians still follow. But as soon as Minos had formed his navy, communication by sea became easier, since he colonized most of the islands and so drove out the wrongdoers. The coast population now applied itself more closely to making money, and its life became more settled. Some even began to build themselves walls, relying on their newly won wealth. For the love of gain made the weaker willing to accept the rule of the stronger, and capital enabled the more powerful to bring the smaller towns into subjection. It was at a somewhat later stage of this development that they went on the expedition against Troy.

In my opinion, what enabled Agamemnon to raise the armament was his superior strength more than the oaths of Tyndareus, which bound the suitors to follow him. Indeed, the account given by those Peloponnesians who have received the most credible tradition runs as follows. First, Pelops came from Asia to a needy population with vast wealth, and acquired such power that, stranger though he was, the country was named after him. Fortune then saw fit to increase this power considerably in the hands of his descendants. Eurystheus had been killed in Attica by the Heraclids. Atreus was his mother’s brother, and when Eurystheus set out on his expedition, he had entrusted Mycenæ and the government to this relation, who had left his father because of the death of Chrysippus. As time went on and Eurystheus did not return, Atreus gave way to the wishes of the Mycenæans, who were influenced by fear of the Heraclids. Besides, his power seemed considerable, and he had not neglected to court the favor of the populace. He then took the scepter of Mycenæ and the rest of the dominions of Eurystheus. So the power of the descendants of Pelops came to be greater than that of the descendants of Perseus. Agamemnon succeeded to all this. He also had a navy far stronger than any of his contemporaries, so that, in my opinion, fear was quite as strong an element as love in forming the confederate expedition. The strength of his navy is shown by the fact that his own contingent was the largest and that he furnished the ships of the Arcadians. This at least is what Homer says, if his testimony is thought sufficient. Besides, in his account of how the scepter was handed down, he calls him
Of many an isle, and of all Argos king.
Now Agamemnon’s was a power on the mainland, and he could not have ruled any islands except the adjacent ones (and these would not be many) unless he had possessed a fleet.

From this expedition we may infer the character of earlier enterprises. Mycenæ may have been a small place, and many of the towns of that age may seem comparatively insignificant. Still, no careful observer would be justified in rejecting, for that reason, the estimate of the armament’s size given by the poets and by tradition. For I suppose that if Lacedaemon became desolate and only the temples and the foundations of the public buildings were left, then as time went on posterity would be strongly inclined to refuse to accept her fame as a true measure of her power. And yet the Lacedaemonians occupy two-fifths of Peloponnese and lead the whole of it, not to speak of their numerous allies outside. Still, the city is not built in a compact form and is not adorned with magnificent temples and public buildings, but is made up of villages after the old fashion of Hellas, and so there would be an impression of inadequacy. If Athens suffered the same misfortune, on the other hand, I suppose that any inference from what the eye saw would make her power appear twice as great as it is. We have therefore no right to be skeptical, nor to be content with looking at a town while ignoring its power. We may safely conclude that the armament in question surpassed all before it, though it fell short of modern efforts, if we can here also accept the testimony of Homer’s poems. Making no allowance for the exaggeration that a poet would feel entitled to use, we can still see in them that it was far from equaling ours. He represents it as consisting of twelve hundred vessels, the Boeotian complement of each ship being a hundred and twenty men and that of the ships of Philoctetes fifty. By this, I conceive, he meant to give the maximum and the minimum complement. At any rate, he does not state the number for any others in his catalogue of the ships. That they were all rowers as well as warriors we see from his account of the ships of Philoctetes, in which all the men at the oar are bowmen. Now it is unlikely that many extra men sailed, except the kings and high officers, especially as they had to cross the open sea with munitions of war, in ships, moreover, that had no decks but were equipped in the old piratical fashion. So if we take the average of the largest and smallest ships, the number of those who sailed appears small, considering that they represented the whole force of Hellas. And this was due not so much to a scarcity of men as to a scarcity of money. Difficulty of supplies made the invaders reduce the army to a size that could live off the country while the war went on. Even after the victory they won on their arrival — and there must have been a victory, or the fortifications of the naval camp could never have been built — there is no sign that their whole force was used. On the contrary, they seem to have turned to cultivating the Chersonese and to piracy for lack of supplies. This is what really enabled the Trojans to keep the field against them for ten years: because the enemy was dispersed, they were always a match for the detachment left behind. If the Hellenes had brought plenty of supplies with them, and had kept up the war without scattering for piracy and agriculture, they would easily have defeated the Trojans in the field, since they could hold their own against them with only the division on service. In short, if they had stuck to the siege, the capture of Troy would have cost them less time and less trouble. But lack of money was the weakness of earlier expeditions, and the same cause affected even this one, more famous than its predecessors. On the evidence of what it accomplished, it may be pronounced inferior to its renown and to the current opinion of it, formed under the teaching of the poets.

Even after the Trojan War, Hellas was still moving and resettling, and so could not reach the quiet that must come before growth. The late return of the Hellenes from Ilium caused many revolutions, and factions arose almost everywhere. It was the citizens driven into exile by them who founded the cities. Sixty years after the capture of Ilium, the Thessalians drove the modern Boeotians out of Arne, and they settled in the present Boeotia, the former Cadmeis. There had been a division of them there before, and some of these had joined the expedition to Ilium. Twenty years later, the Dorians and the Heraclids became masters of Peloponnese. So much had to be done, and so many years had to pass, before Hellas could reach a lasting tranquility free from removals and could begin to send out colonies. Athens sent them to Ionia and most of the islands, and the Peloponnesians to most of Italy and Sicily and some places in the rest of Hellas. All these places were founded after the war with Troy.

But as the power of Hellas grew and the acquisition of wealth became more of an object, the revenues of the states increased, and through them tyrannies were established almost everywhere — the old form of government having been hereditary monarchy with defined prerogatives. Hellas then began to fit out fleets and to apply herself more closely to the sea. It is said that the Corinthians were the first to approach the modern style of naval architecture, and that Corinth was the first place in Hellas where galleys were built. We find Ameinocles, a Corinthian shipwright, building four ships for the Samians. Counting from the end of this war, it is nearly three hundred years since Ameinocles went to Samos. Again, the earliest sea-fight in history was between the Corinthians and Corcyraeans, about two hundred and sixty years ago, counting from the same time. Corinth, planted on an isthmus, had been a commercial center from time out of mind. In former times almost all communication between the Hellenes inside and outside Peloponnese went overland, and the Corinthian territory was the highway it traveled by. She therefore had great money resources, as the old poets show by the epithet “wealthy” which they gave to the place. This enabled her, when traffic by sea became more common, to acquire her navy and put down piracy. Since she could offer a market for both branches of the trade, she gained all the power that a large revenue affords. Later the Ionians attained great naval strength, in the reign of Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, and of his son Cambyses. While they were at war with Cyrus, they commanded the Ionian sea for a time. Polycrates also, the tyrant of Samos, had a powerful navy in the reign of Cambyses, with which he subdued many of the islands, among them Rhenea, which he consecrated to the Delian Apollo. About this time also the Phocaeans, while founding Marseilles, defeated the Carthaginians in a sea-fight. These were the most powerful navies. And even these, although so many generations had passed since the Trojan war, seem to have consisted mainly of the old fifty-oared ships and long-boats, with few galleys among them. Indeed it was only shortly before the Persian war and the death of Darius, the successor of Cambyses, that the Sicilian tyrants and the Corcyraeans acquired any large number of galleys. For after these there were no navies of any account in Hellas until the expedition of Xerxes. Aegina, Athens, and others may have had a few vessels, but they were mostly fifty-oared ships. It was quite at the end of this period that the war with Aegina and the prospect of the barbarian invasion enabled Themistocles to persuade the Athenians to build the fleet with which they fought at Salamis, and even these vessels did not have complete decks.

The navies of the Hellenes during the period we have covered were, then, what I have described. Their insignificance did not prevent them from being a source of the greatest power for those who cultivated them, in revenue and in dominion alike. They were the means by which the islands were reached and subdued, those of the smallest area falling most easily. There were no wars by land, at least none by which power was acquired. We hear of the usual border contests, but of distant expeditions aimed at conquest we hear nothing among the Hellenes. No subject cities gathered round a great state, and no equals combined of their own accord for confederate expeditions. What fighting there was consisted merely of local warfare between rival neighbors. The nearest approach to a coalition came in the old war between Chalcis and Eretria, a quarrel in which the rest of the Hellenic name did to some extent take sides.

The national growth also met various obstacles in various localities. The power of the Ionians was advancing rapidly when it collided with Persia under King Cyrus. Cyrus dethroned Croesus and overran everything between the Halys and the sea, and he did not stop until he had reduced the cities of the coast. Only the islands were left to be subdued by Darius and the Phoenician navy.

Again, wherever there were tyrants, their habit was to provide simply for themselves, looking solely to their personal comfort and the aggrandizement of their families. This made safety the great aim of their policy and kept anything great from coming from them, though each would have his own affairs with his immediate neighbors. All this is true only of the mother country, for in Sicily the tyrants attained very great power. Thus for a long time everywhere in Hellas we find causes that left the states equally incapable of combining for great and national ends, or of any vigorous action of their own.

But at last a time came when Lacedaemon, once and for all, put down the tyrants of Athens and the far older tyrannies of the rest of Hellas, except those in Sicily. This city had suffered from factions for an unparalleled length of time after the settlement of the Dorians, its present inhabitants. Still, at a very early period it obtained good laws and enjoyed an unbroken freedom from tyrants. It has had the same form of government for more than four hundred years, reckoning to the end of the late war, and has thus been in a position to arrange the affairs of the other states. Not many years after the deposition of the tyrants, the battle of Marathon was fought between the Medes and the Athenians. Ten years afterwards, the barbarian returned with the armada to subjugate Hellas. In the face of this great danger, the Lacedaemonians took command of the confederate Hellenes by virtue of their superior power. The Athenians, having made up their minds to abandon their city, broke up their homes, threw themselves into their ships, and became a naval people. This coalition repulsed the barbarian, but soon afterwards split into two sections, which included the Hellenes who had revolted from the King as well as those who had aided him in the war. At the head of one stood Athens, at the head of the other Lacedaemon, the first naval and the first military power in Hellas. For a short time the league held together, until the Lacedaemonians and Athenians quarreled and made war on each other with their allies. Into this duel all the Hellenes were drawn sooner or later, though some might at first remain neutral. So the whole period from the Median war to this one, with some peaceful intervals, was spent by each power in war, either with its rival or with its own revolted allies. It therefore gave them constant practice in military matters, and that experience which is learned in the school of danger.

The policy of Lacedaemon was not to exact tribute from her allies, but merely to secure their subservience to her interests by establishing oligarchies among them. Athens, on the contrary, had by degrees taken away her allies’ ships and imposed contributions of money instead on all of them except Chios and Lesbos. Each of them separately found its resources for this war greater than the sum of their strength when the alliance flourished intact.

Having now given the results of my inquiries into early times, I grant that it will be hard to believe every particular detail. Most men deal with traditions, even traditions of their own country, by accepting them all alike as they are handed down, without applying any critical test whatever. The general Athenian public imagine that Hipparchus was tyrant when he fell by the hands of Harmodius and Aristogiton. They do not know that Hippias, the eldest of the sons of Pisistratus, was really supreme, and that Hipparchus and Thessalus were his brothers. On the very day, indeed at the very moment fixed for the deed, Harmodius and Aristogiton suspected that their accomplices had given information to Hippias. They concluded that he had been warned and did not attack him. Yet, not liking to be arrested and to risk their lives for nothing, they fell on Hipparchus near the temple of the daughters of Leos and killed him as he was arranging the Panathenaic procession.

There are many other unfounded ideas current among the rest of the Hellenes, even on matters of contemporary history that time has not obscured. For instance, there is the notion that the Lacedaemonian kings have two votes each, when in fact they have only one, and that there is a company of Pitane, when there is simply no such thing. So little trouble do the common people take in investigating the truth, readily accepting the first story that comes to hand. On the whole, however, I believe the conclusions I have drawn from the proofs quoted may safely be relied on. They will certainly not be disturbed either by the lays of a poet, displaying the exaggeration of his craft, or by the compositions of the chroniclers, which are attractive at the expense of truth. The subjects these treat of are beyond the reach of evidence, and time has robbed most of them of historical value by placing them in the region of legend. Turning from these, we can rest satisfied with having proceeded on the clearest data, and with having reached conclusions as exact as can be expected in matters of such antiquity. To come to this war: the actors in a struggle are known to overrate its importance, and when it is over to return to admiring earlier events. Despite this, an examination of the facts will show that it was much greater than the wars that preceded it.

With reference to the speeches in this history, some were delivered before the war began, others while it was going on. Some I heard myself, others I got from various quarters. In all cases it was difficult to carry them word for word in one’s memory, so my habit has been to make the speakers say what was in my opinion demanded of them by the various occasions, while adhering as closely as possible to the general sense of what they really said. As for the narrative of events, I did not permit myself to take it from the first source that came to hand, and I did not even trust my own impressions. It rests partly on what I saw myself and partly on what others saw for me, and I always tested the accuracy of the report by the most severe and detailed tests possible. My conclusions cost me some labor, because different eye-witnesses gave accounts of the same events that did not agree. This arose sometimes from imperfect memory, sometimes from undue partiality for one side or the other. The absence of romance in my history will, I fear, detract somewhat from its interest. But if it is judged useful by those inquirers who want an exact knowledge of the past as an aid to interpreting the future, which in the course of human things must resemble it if it does not reflect it, I shall be content. In short, I have written my work not as an essay to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time.

The Median War, the greatest achievement of past times, was nevertheless decided quickly, in two actions by sea and two by land. The Peloponnesian War was prolonged to an immense length, and long as it was, it was short without parallel for the misfortunes it brought upon Hellas. Never had so many cities been taken and laid desolate, some by the barbarians and some by the parties contending (the old inhabitants being sometimes removed to make room for others). Never was there so much banishing and bloodshed, now on the field of battle, now in the strife of faction. Old stories of events handed down by tradition, but scarcely confirmed by experience, suddenly ceased to be incredible. There were earthquakes of unparalleled extent and violence, and eclipses of the sun occurred more often than is recorded for any earlier time. There were great droughts in various places with the famines that followed, and that most calamitous and terribly deadly visitation, the plague. All this came upon them along with the late war, which the Athenians and Peloponnesians began by dissolving the thirty years’ truce made after the conquest of Euboea. To the question why they broke the treaty, I answer by first setting out their grounds of complaint and points of difference, so that no one may ever have to ask what immediate cause plunged the Hellenes into a war of such magnitude. The real cause I consider to be the one that was formally kept most out of sight. The growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable. Still it is well to give the grounds alleged by either side that led to the dissolution of the treaty and the outbreak of the war.
